title: Act III, Scene V
focus: parting at dawn and Capulet's rage

teacherSummary.text: At dawn the lovers argue whether it is the nightingale or the lark. Romeo leaves. Lady Capulet tells Juliet of the wedding; Juliet refuses. Capulet threatens to throw her out. The Nurse advises marrying Paris; Juliet decides to seek the Friar's help, or die.

vocabulary.context:
Wife, we scarce thought us blest
That God had lent us but this only child;
But now I see this one is one too much,
And that we have a curse in having her:
Out on her, hilding!

No nightingale: look, love, what envious streaks
Do lace the severing clouds in yonder east:
Night’s candles are burnt out, and jocund day
Stands tiptoe on the misty mountain tops.

segments.script: First, meaning. I read “It was the nightingale, and not the lark” slowly and put it in my own words: At dawn, Juliet insists the bird they heard was the nightingale, not the lark, so Romeo can stay. Next, craft. I notice the contrast of bird images, the night-singing nightingale against the morning lark. The strongest word is “nightingale”: it sings at night, so it would mean day has not yet come. Then, effect. Why does Juliet insist it was the nightingale? My answer: Juliet wants to delay their parting because dawn means Romeo must flee or die; the lovers' happiness belongs to darkness, and daylight brings danger.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the scene to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.

contentNotes.teacherNote: Capulet threatens to throw Juliet into the streets and calls her names; at the end Juliet says that if all else fails she has the power to die. Use the safe-messaging script; keep discussion on power, choice and where she could turn. This is the morning after the wedding night: the marriage has been consummated, and Juliet is not yet fourteen. Name her age plainly, set it against Elizabethan norms (most English brides were in their twenties), and discuss the pressure on her to marry Paris as coercion.
contentNotes.studentPreview: A father threatens his daughter, and she speaks of dying. Support is available if this is hard to read. A thirteen-year-old is pressured to marry after a secret marriage.
contentNotes.suggestedLanguage: “What options does Juliet have, and who could help her?”

safeMessaging.teacherScript: Discuss the character's despair and what the text does with it; do not dwell on methods. Before the lesson, remind students that support is available and how to reach the counselor. Check in privately with any student who seems affected and follow your school's referral protocol.
